claim: Drosophila compound eyes are composed of ~750 seemingly regular lens-capped modules called ommatidia
source: The Drosophila compound eyes are composed of ~750 seemingly regular lens-capped modules called ommatidia, which should provide the fly a panoramic visual field of low optical resolution (Barlow, 1952; Land, 1997).
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about Drosophila eyes, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Each ommatidium contains eight photoreceptor cells (R1-R8), pointing to seven different directions
source: Each ommatidium contains eight photoreceptor cells (R1-R8), pointing to seven different directions.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about ommatidium structure.

claim: R1-R6 photoreceptors are ultraviolet and blue-green-sensitive outer photoreceptors that initiate the motion vision pathway
source: The ultraviolet and blue-green-sensitive outer photoreceptors, R1-R6, initiate the motion vision pathway, whilst the central R7 and R8, which lie on top of each other, detect different colors from one direction (Wardill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wardill et al., 2012.

claim: The average interommatidial angle in Drosophila is Δφ = 4.5°
source: the photoreceptor spacing (spatial resolution) effectively matches the ommatidium spacing (average interommatidial angle, Δφ = 4.5o (Götz, 1964; Land, 1997; Gonzalez-Bellido et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations providing the measurement.

claim: R1-R6 photoreceptors capture 2-to-4-times more information in time than previous maximum estimates when responding to high-contrast bursts
source: Our intracellular recordings reveal that R1-R6s capture 2-to-4-times more information in time than previous maximum estimates (Juusola and Hardie, 2001a; Song et al., 2012; Song and Juusola, 2014) when responding to high-contrast bursts (periods of rapid light changes followed by quiescent periods) that resemble light input from natural scenes generated by saccadic viewing.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and comparison to previous estimates from cited work.

claim: High-contrast bursts resemble light input from natural scenes generated by saccadic viewing
source: when responding to high-contrast bursts (periods of rapid light changes followed by quiescent periods) that resemble light input from natural scenes generated by saccadic viewing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing similarity between burst stimuli and natural saccadic viewing patterns.

claim: Interspersed 'fixation' intervals allow photoreceptors to sample more information from phasic light changes by relieving them from refractoriness
source: Biophysically-realistic model simulations suggest that this improvement largely results from interspersed 'fixation' intervals, which allow photoreceptors to sample more information from phasic light changes by relieving them from refractoriness (Song et al., 2012; Song and Juusola, 2014; Juusola et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by model simulations and citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Photomechanical photoreceptor contractions work together with refractory sampling to improve spatial acuity
source: Remarkably, over space, our intracellular recordings, high-speed microscopy and modeling further reveal how photomechanical photoreceptor contractions (Hardie and Franze, 2012) work together with refractory sampling to improve spatial acuity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental approaches (recordings, microscopy, modeling) and citation to prior work on photomechanical contractions.

claim: Photomechanical processes reduce motion blur during saccades and adaptation during gaze fixation
source: We discover that by actively modulating light input and photoreceptor output, these processes reduce motion blur during saccades and adaptation during gaze fixation, which otherwise could fade vision (Ditchburn and Ginsborg, 1952; Riggs and Ratliff, 1952; Land, 1997).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and citations to prior work on visual fading.

claim: Phasic responses sharpen retinal images by highlighting the times when visual objects cross a photoreceptor's receptive field, thereby encoding space in time
source: The resulting phasic responses sharpen retinal images by highlighting the times when visual objects cross a photoreceptor's receptive field, thereby encoding space in time (see also: Ahissar and Arieli, 2001; Donner and Hemilä, 2007; Rucci et al., 2007; Kuang et al., 2012a; Kuang et al., 2012; Franceschini et al., 2014; Viollet, 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and citations to related work in other systems.

claim: Neither saccades nor fixations blind the flies, but together improve vision
source: Thus, neither saccades nor fixations blind the flies, but together improve vision.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about photomechanical processes and information sampling.

claim: Drosophila can see >4 fold finer details than their eyes' spatial sampling limit
source: Incorporation of this novel opto-mechano-electric mechanism into our 'microsaccadic sampling'-model predicts that Drosophila can see >4 fold finer details than their eyes' spatial sampling limit – a prediction directly confirmed by optomotor behavior experiments.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by both model predictions and behavioral experiments.

claim: The acuity of an eye is limited by its photoreceptor spacing, which provides the grain of the retinal image
source: The acuity of an eye is limited by its photoreceptor spacing, which provides the grain of the retinal image.
evidence: This is established knowledge in vision science.

claim: To resolve two stationary objects, at least three photoreceptors are needed for detecting the intensity difference in between
source: To resolve two stationary objects, at least three photoreceptors are needed for detecting the intensity difference in between.
evidence: This is established knowledge in vision science about spatial resolution limits.

claim: Resolving two moving objects is harder than stationary objects because vision becomes further limited by each photoreceptor's finite integration time and receptive field size
source: To resolve two moving objects is harder, as vision becomes further limited by each photoreceptor's finite integration time and receptive field size (Srinivasan and Bernard, 1975; Juusola and French, 1997; Land, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Animals from insects to man view the world by using saccades and fixation intervals
source: Nevertheless, animals - from insects to man - view the world by using saccades, fast movements, which direct their eyes to the surroundings, and fixation intervals between the saccades, during which gaze is held near stationary (Land, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual behavior across species, supported by citation.

claim: Fast adaptation causes perceptual fading during fixation
source: A well-known trade-off of fast adaptation is that it causes perceptual fading during fixation (Ditchburn and Ginsborg, 1952; Riggs and Ratliff, 1952)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to classic studies.

claim: To see the world requires motion or self-motion: body, head and eye movements
source: and to see the world requires motion or self-motion: body, head and eye movements (Hengstenberg, 1971; Land, 1973; Franceschini and Chagneux, 1997; Schilstra and van Hateren, 1998; Blaj and van Hateren, 2004; Martinez-Conde et al., 2013), which remove adaptation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: R1-R6 photoreceptors responded most vigorously to high-contrast bursts containing fast transient events with darker intervals
source: Intracellular recordings (Figure 1A) revealed that photoreceptors responded most vigorously to high-contrast bursts, which contained fast transient events with darker intervals.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1.

claim: The slowest high-contrast bursts (20 Hz) evoked the largest peak-to-peak responses (43.4 ± 5.6 mV; mean ± SD, n = 16 cells)
source: Therefore, the slowest high-contrast bursts (red; top-left) with the longest darker intervals, which theoretically (Song et al., 2012; Song and Juusola, 2014; Juusola et al., 2015) should relieve most refractory microvilli (Appendixes 1–3), evoked the largest peak-to-peak responses (43.4 ± 5.6 mV; mean ± SD, n = 16 cells; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with quantitative measurements.

claim: The fastest low-contrast GWN evoked the smallest responses (3.7 ± 1.1 mV; n = 4)
source: Whereas the fastest low-contrast GWN (blue; bottom-right), which would keep more microvilli refractory, evoked the smallest responses (3.7 ± 1.1 mV; n = 4).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with quantitative measurements.

claim: The maximum signal power spectra to bursty stimuli could be up to ~6,000 times larger than that of the noise
source: The maximum signal power spectra to bursty stimuli could be up to ~6,000 times larger than that of the noise, which was effectively stimulus-invariant (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Information transfer peaked at 100 Hz bursts
source: Accordingly, signaling performance (Figure 2A,C) increased both with the stimulus bandwidth (left) and contrast (right), until these became too fast to follow. Information transfer peaked at 100 Hz bursts, which allocated the R1-R6's limited bandwidth and amplitude range near-optimally
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 2.

claim: A photoreceptor's information transfer to 100 Hz bursts was 610–850 bits/s
source: Remarkably, this performance (610–850 bits/s) was 2-to-4-times of that for GWN (200–350 bits/s), which has often been used for characterizing maximal encoding (Juusola and Hardie, 2001a), and twice of that for rich naturalistic stimuli (380–510 bits/s) (Song and Juusola, 2014) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with quantitative measurements comparing different stimulus types.

claim: The biophysically realistic photoreceptor model transferred 633 ± 20 bits/s at its peak for 100 Hz bursts
source: At its peak, the model transferred 633 ± 20 bits/s (mean ± SD; Figure 4C) for 100 Hz bursts of 8 × 105 photons/s
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations with quantitative measurements.

claim: Real R1-R6s receive extra information from their neighbors through superposition
source: The real R1-R6s, on balance, receive extra information from their neighbors (Rivera-Alba et al., 2011; Wardill et al., 2012), which through superposition (Zheng et al., 2006) sample information from overlapping receptive fields.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on neural connectivity and inference from the data.

claim: R6 photoreceptors have large rhabdomeres and gap-junctions to R8
source: Here, R6s, with large rhabdomeres (Figure 5B) and gap-junctions to R8 (Figure 5C), should receive the most (Wardill et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5 and citation.

claim: A locomoting Drosophila generates ~1–5 head/body-saccades/s
source: A locomoting Drosophila generates ~1–5 head/body-saccades/s, which direct its gaze in high velocities to the surroundings (Fry et al., 2003; Geurten et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila behavior supported by citations.

claim: Saccadic viewing of natural images transformed the resulting light input to resemble bursty high-contrast stimulation
source: We found that saccadic viewing of natural images (Figure 6C,i), even without visual selection (i.e. without the fly choosing what it gazes), transformed the resulting light input to resemble the bursty high-contrast stimulation (Video 1), which maximized photoreceptor information (Figures 1–2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 6 and Video 1.

claim: Saccadic walks contained fixation periods that retained the same light input values for longer durations than linear walks
source: Specifically, the saccadic walks contained fixation periods that retained the same light input values for longer durations than the linear walks, which lacked these periods, causing the ~63% higher peak in the saccadic histogram (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Saccadic walking enhanced the proportion of large intensity differences by ~18% higher histogram flanks than linear walking
source: Saccadic walking also enhanced the proportion of large intensity differences between two consecutive moments, seen as ~18% higher histogram flanks than those for linear walking (p=3.65 × 10−9, pair-wise t-test for the combined 0.5–1.0 and -0.5--1 ranges).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with quantitative statistical analysis.

claim: Dark-adapted wild-type R1-R6 photoreceptors' mean acceptance angle was ∆ρdark = 9.47 ± 1.57°, n = 19 cells
source: Importantly, the dots' angular separation was less than the half-width of a R1-R6's receptive field (Figure 7C) at the two backgrounds (∆ρdark = 9.47 ± 1.57°, n = 19 cells; ∆ρlight = 7.70 ± 1.27°, n = 6; mean ± SD; Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement of receptive field size.

claim: Light-adapted wild-type R1-R6 photoreceptors' mean acceptance angle was ∆ρlight = 7.70 ± 1.27°, n = 6
source: Importantly, the dots' angular separation was less than the half-width of a R1-R6's receptive field (Figure 7C) at the two backgrounds (∆ρdark = 9.47 ± 1.57°, n = 19 cells; ∆ρlight = 7.70 ± 1.27°, n = 6; mean ± SD; Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: This is a primary experimental measurement of receptive field size.

claim: Recordings showed distinctive responses to two fast-moving dots as two peaks separated by a trough
source: Remarkably in all these tests, the recordings showed distinctive responses to the two dots (Figure 7B), as two peaks separated by a trough.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Volterra-model predictions failed to resolve the double-fast dots, instead blurring into one broad response
source: However, in marked contrast, the model predictions failed to resolve the double-fast dots, instead blurring into one broad response in both adapting states (Figure 7D; blue vs. black bars, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations compared to experimental data.

claim: A photoreceptor's real resolving power was significantly better and less affected by motion blur than predicted by classic theory
source: Thus, a photoreceptor's real resolving power was significantly better and less affected by motion blur than predicted by classic theory (Appendix 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing experimental data to theoretical predictions.

claim: hdcJK910 R1-R6s resolved the dots at least equally well as the wild-type
source: Instead, we found that hdcJK910 R1-R6s resolved the dots at least equally well as the wild-type (Figure 7D, red).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding comparing mutant and wild-type photoreceptors.

claim: High acuity did not result from synaptic inputs but was intrinsic to photoreceptors
source: Thus, high acuity did not result from synaptic inputs but was intrinsic to photoreceptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the hdcJK910 mutant experiments.

claim: R1-R6 recordings often showed phasic directional selectivity, with responses rising and decaying faster to back-to-front than to front-to-back moving dots
source: We further discovered that R1-R6 recordings often showed phasic directional selectivity (Figure 7G), with the responses rising and decaying faster to back-to-front than to front-to-back moving dots.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Atomic-force microscopy has revealed minute (<275 nm) vertical movements on the surface of dissected Drosophila eyes generated by contraction of individual microvilli
source: Namely, atomic-force microscopy has revealed minute (<275 nm) vertical movements on the surface of dissected Drosophila eyes, generated by contraction of individual microvilli as PIP2 is hydrolyzed from the inner leaflet of the lipid bilayer (Hardie and Franze, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Rhabdomeres moved 8–20 ms after a flash onset, being maximally displaced 70–200 ms later
source: We found that 8–20 ms after a flash the rhabdomeres, which directly faced the light source at the image center, shifted rapidly towards the anterior side of their ommatidia (Figure 8B). These local movements were faster and larger the brighter the flash (Figure 8C), and reached their intensity-dependent maxima (0.2–1.2 µm; Figure 8D) in 70–200 ms, before returning more slowly to their original positions
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from high-speed video recordings shown in Figure 8.

claim: A bright flash could shift a rhabdomere more than its half-width sideways
source: Because the mean R1-R6 rhabdomere tip diameter is ~1.7 µm (Figure 5B), a bright flash could shift it more than its half-width sideways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing movement measurements to anatomical measurements.

claim: Light-activated rhabdomeres moved in back-to-front direction along the eye's equatorial (anterior-posterior) plane
source: Video footage at different eye locations indicated that light-activated rhabdomeres moved in back-to-front direction along the eye's equatorial (anterior-posterior) plane (Figure 8E, red; Video 3), with little up-down components (black).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from video analysis.

claim: The ommatidium lens stayed nearly still during rhabdomere movements
source: Crucially, we found that the ommatidium lens stayed nearly still, while specific pigment and cone cells, which are connected to the rhabdomere tips by adherens junctions (Tepass and Harris, 2007), formed a narrow aperture that moved with the rhabdomeres but only half as much.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from z-axis scanning shown in Figure 8F and Video 4.

claim: Rhabdomeres moved ~ 2 times more than the aperture formed by cone and pigment cells, and ~ 10 times more than the lens
source: Rhabdomeres moved ~ 2 times more than this aperture, and ~ 10 times more than the lens.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding with quantitative comparison shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The microsaccadic sampling model's output closely predicted the responses to two moving dots
source: Crucially, with such input driving the refractory photon sampling model, its output (iv) closely predicted the responses to the two moving dots (Figure 8I and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from model simulations that match experimental data.

claim: Early behavioral experiments in bright illumination suggested R1-R6 acceptance angles of ~3.5°
source: Interestingly, early behavioral experiments in bright illumination (Götz, 1964) suggested similarly narrow R1-R6 acceptance angles (~3.5o).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior behavioral work, supported by citation.

claim: If dots or a Drosophila moved at 10 o/s, a photoreceptor should resolve image details at 1° resolution
source: We found that if the dots, or a Drosophila, moved at suitable speed, a photoreceptor should resolve them well (Figure 9A), with this performance depending upon the inter-dot-distance. When the dots/eye moved at 10 o/s, a R1-R6 may capture image details at 1o resolution.
evidence: This is a prediction from the microsaccadic sampling model shown in Figure 9.

claim: 3°-apart-dots should be seen at 5–100 o/s speeds and 4°-apart-dots even during fast saccades (200–300 o/s)
source: Conversely, 3o-apart-dots should be seen at 5–100 o/s speeds and 4o-apart-dots even during fast saccades (200–300 o/s).
evidence: This is a prediction from the microsaccadic sampling model.

claim: Intracellular recordings corroborated the microsaccadic sampling model predictions
source: Again, intracellular recordings corroborated these predictions (Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1), demonstrating how acuity could be enhanced by encoding space in time.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding that validates model predictions.

claim: Every tested fly responded to hyperacute (<4.5°) bar stimuli consistently
source: We found that every tested fly responded down to ~1o panoramic bar resolution (Figure 10A and Figure 10—figure supplement 1) with their responses becoming smaller the finer its bars (Figure 10A–C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from optomotor behavior experiments.

claim: Optomotor responses consistently followed the rotation direction changes, indicating they were not caused by aliasing
source: Importantly, because these responses consistently followed the rotation direction changes, they were not caused by aliasing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Optomotor behavior verified that Drosophila see the world at least in 4-fold finer detail than what was previously thought
source: Thus, optomotor behavior verified that Drosophila see the world at least in 4-fold finer detail than what was previously thought.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral experiments.

claim: When a fine-grained (3.9°) panoramic image was rotated faster, the optomotor response declined as predicted
source: Moreover, when a fine-grained (3.9o) panoramic image was rotated faster (Figure 10D), the response declined as predicted (cf. two dots 4o apart in Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding that matches model predictions.

claim: Drosophila see hyperacute details even at saccadic speeds
source: This result is consistent with photoreceptor output setting the perceptual limit for vision and demonstrates that Drosophila see hyperacute details even at saccadic speeds (Figure 10D–F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral experiments at different speeds.

claim: The dynamic interplay between saccades and gaze fixation is important for both the maintenance and enhancement of vision already at the photoreceptor level
source: Our results indicate that the dynamic interplay between saccades and gaze fixation is important for both the maintenance and enhancement of vision already at the photoreceptor level.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from all the experimental findings.

claim: Light input is first regulated by two processes inside photoreceptors: slower screening pigment migration (intracellular pupil, 1–10 s) and much faster photomechanical rhabdomere contractions (0.01–1 s)
source: Light input is first regulated by two processes inside photoreceptors: slower screening pigment migration (intracellular pupil, 1–10 s) and much faster photomechanical rhabdomere contractions (0.01–1 s).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about photomechanical processes.

claim: Photomechanical modulations have low noise
source: These modulations have low noise (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), enabling refractory photon sampling by microvilli to enhance information intake in phasic stimulus components.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Over space, photomechanical mechanisms sharpen neural resolvability by ~4 fold below the theoretical limit of the compound eye optics
source: Remarkably, over space, these mechanisms further sharpen neural resolvability by ~4 fold below the theoretical limit of the compound eye optics, providing hyperacute vision.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the spatial acuity experiments.

claim: With microsaccadic sampling, a fly's behavioral decisions govern its visual information/acuity trade-off
source: Thus, with microsaccadic sampling, a fly's behavioral decisions govern its visual information/acuity trade-off.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: To see the finest image details a fly should scan the world slowly, which probably happens during normal gaze fixation
source: To see the finest image details it should scan the world slowly, which probably happens during normal gaze fixation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model predictions and experimental data.

claim: By locomoting faster, in a saccadic or bursty fashion, visual information capture in time is increased while surprisingly little spatial details about surroundings would be lost
source: Conversely, by locomoting faster, in a saccadic or bursty fashion, visual information capture in time is increased (see also: Juusola and de Polavieja, 2003), while surprisingly little spatial details about its surroundings would be lost.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, supported by citation.

claim: The extraction of phasic stimulus features, which characterize object boundaries and line elements in visual scenes, already starts during sampling and integration of visual information in the microvilli
source: Interestingly, here our findings further imply that, in Drosophila, the extraction of phasic stimulus features, which characterize object boundaries and line elements in visual scenes, already starts during sampling and integration of visual information in the microvilli, at the first processing stage (rather than later on in the retinal network or in the brain).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about photoreceptor function.

claim: Animals should fixate gaze on darker features to resensitize photoreceptors by relieving their refractory sampling units
source: Animals should fixate gaze on darker features, as this resensitizes photoreceptors by relieving their refractory sampling units (e.g. microvilli).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings about refractory sampling.

claim: Animals should rapidly move gaze across to brighter image areas, as saccadic crossings over high-contrast boundaries enhance information intake
source: And then, rapidly move gaze across to brighter image areas, as saccadic crossings over high-contrast boundaries enhance information intake by increasing photoreceptors' sample (quantum bump) rate changes/time (Appendix 9).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the experimental findings about information sampling.

claim: If information sampling biophysics in rods and cones were matched to microsaccadic eye movements, this could provide a mechanistic explanation to how saccadic gaze fixation provides stable perception while curtailing motion blur effects
source: Therefore, if information sampling biophysics in rods and cones were matched to microsaccadic eye movements, this could provide a mechanistic explanation to the old paradox: how saccadic gaze fixation provides stable perception of the world, while curtailing motion blur effects.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to vertebrate vision.
